  • Verlo, a provider of an AI operating system built for wealth management firms, has secured $4.5m CAD in seed funding to help Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) cut back on time-consuming administrative tasks.
  • In a recent development, staircase Ventures led the investment, while Pelorus VC came back to back the manufacturer again.
  • The firm says its technology gives RIAs and wealth managers the groundwork they need to reclaim thousands of hours otherwise lost to admin, allowing them to expand their client base without taking on extra operational costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Verlo, a provider of an AI operating system built for wealth management firms, has secured $4.5m CAD in seed funding to help Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) cut back on time-consuming administrative tasks.

In a recent development, staircase Ventures led the investment, while Pelorus VC came back to back the manufacturer again. They were joined by several angel investors, among them founders and senior executives from Verafin, the Newfoundland financial crime software business that Nasdaq bought in 2020 for $2.7bn.

The firm says its technology gives RIAs and wealth managers the groundwork they need to reclaim thousands of hours otherwise lost to admin, allowing them to expand their client base without taking on extra operational costs.

Verlo intends to put the fresh capital towards enhancing its platform, growing its headcount in St. John’s and speeding up its expansion in the US.

Industry observers note that the business describes itself as a compliant AI operating system for the wealth sector. It turns every client record and interaction into material that AI agents can search and draw upon, enabling RIAs to automate administrative work, build their books of business and oversee AI use across the whole firm, while saving time and avoiding added overhead. To achieve this, Verlo brings together and reconciles information from a firm’s custodian, CRM, document storage, calendar and email into one trusted dataset for its agents.

Verlo CEO and founder Brent Pretty remarked, “Our customers are independent advisors and wealth management firms who are weighed down by tedious admin. Verlo is the AI operating system that frees up their time to focus on growth, not paperwork.”.

He added, “Legacy wealth management tools are beginning to introduce AI, but they feel more like add-ons to existing workflows rather than integrated technology that will fundamentally transform how their firm operates. They keep data siloed, which sets AI agents up for failure. Any answers they give will be useless because the source can’t be trusted.”.

Industry observers note that staircase Ventures managing partner Janet Bannister stated, “Verlo has the product, team and traction to win. When we met Brent, we were immediately impressed by his tenacity, vision, bias for action, and understanding of the nuances of building great products in heavily regulated industries. The team is dedicated to helping wealth management firms stay focused on their clients by reducing their administrative overhead.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Product Lead, Google Cloud Dedicated.

Product Manager, Google Cloud Dedicated.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Across Europe, organizations handling sensitive workloads in regulated sectors — such as financial services, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and the public sector — are trying to modernize their infrastructure while adhering to strict local data governance standards, including SecNumCloud in France and BSI C3A in Germany.

To help organizations accomplish this, Google Cloud Dedicated provides the architectural, security, and API consistency of Google Cloud in locally governed environments managed by independent domestic operators. But infrastructure is only the starting point. Organizations also need to transform the software ecosystem they rely on every day.

To meet regional sovereignty requirements, organizations acquire and run these software solutions through trusted local entities — such as S3NS in France (a joint venture majority-owned and managed by Thales) and a newly formed German entity that will also be owned and managed by Thales, currently in preview. These local entities operate dedicated infrastructure stacks, help maintain operational custody, and handle customer data within independent jurisdictional boundaries.

Today, we are highlighting the expanding independent software vendor (ISV) ecosystem validated on Google Cloud Dedicated, enabling French and German organizations to run their critical enterprise software in environments designed to support their sovereign and regulatory needs.

Deploying in a sovereign boundary should not require an organization to sacrifice software choice or rewrite its enterprise applications.Because Google Cloud Dedicated provides architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, validated enterprise software runs directly inside these partner-operated environments without custom re-platforming.

This model provides European enterprises with three concrete advantages:.

Localized operational custody: Infrastructure operations, software quarantine procedures, and day-to-day administrative access are under the direct management of local European partners operating with specialized remote technical escalations governed by strict, partner-supervised escorted access controls.

Broad software choice: Regulated institutions can deploy industry-standard tools for identity governance, cyber resilience, simulation, and data streaming natively in their sovereign perimeter.

Streamlined compliance: Organizations fulfill national frameworks like SecNumCloud and BSI guidelines while preserving familiar CI/CD pipelines, APIs, and developer workflows.

When highly regulated European institutions consider moving to a sovereign cloud, the infrastructure itself is rarely the primary roadblock. The real bottleneck is software.Historically, pursuing strict sovereignty meant accepting compromises:.

Rewriting applications from scratch or maintaining custom, brittle tooling because mainstream enterprise platforms were unavailable.

Forcing security, engineering, and data teams to abandon the industry-standard tools they use daily in favor of untested niche alternatives.

Sidelining high-impact initiatives like real-time fraud scoring, automated DevSecOps, and modern identity governance simply because the required ISVs could not legally or technically operate in the environment.

Sources indicate that because Google Cloud Dedicated maintains architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, leading global and European software providers can deploy their proven platforms directly inside national, domestic operator-managed boundaries. Regulated organizations retain the software, automated pipelines, and operational standards they rely on — without sacrificing compliance or operational custody.

In a recent development, deploying enterprise software on Google Cloud Dedicated and S3NS isn't just about hosting an application locally; it’s about pairing proven software engines with sovereign operations. Here is how these joint architectures unlock strategic value for European enterprises:.

Recent findings suggest that cohesity on Google Cloud Dedicated (Sovereign cyber resilience): Cohesity has many options to meet organizational data sovereignty objectives, whether on-premises or in the cloud with Google Cloud Dedicated. This is done through a unified, cyber resilient, AI-powered data platform — Cohesity Data Cloud — that is sovereign-by-design, making it easier to protect, manage, recover, and have visibility into data, while supporting compliance with data sovereignty requirements. For example, running Cohesity directly in the S3NS perimeter combines Cohesity’s Zero Trust cyber resilience architecture designed for immutability with local operational custody. Customers gain advanced threat hunting, cyber vaulting, and recovery orchestration that powers quick, clean, and trusted cyber-recovery from ransomware threats without allowing diagnostic telemetry, secondary backup copies, or operational keys to traverse external networks.

GitLab on Google Cloud Dedicated (Secure, compliant software delivery pipelines): Combining GitLab’s DevSecOps platform with Google Cloud Dedicated allows defense, aerospace, and public sector engineering teams to ship code at commercial velocity. Proprietary source code, vulnerability scans, and CI/CD artifact registries stay contained behind the partner-operated boundary, significantly reducing audit friction of using public SaaS code repositories.

Ansys, part of Synopsys, on Google Cloud Dedicated (High-performance sovereign engineering simulation): Pairing Ansys, part of Synopsys, high-performance computing simulation workflows with the dedicated compute clusters of Google Cloud Dedicated gives European manufacturers the massive scale needed for aerodynamic, fluid, and structural modeling. Highly sensitive intellectual property, blueprints, and digital twins designed to keep intellectual property within regional boundaries and national jurisdiction while running at cloud speed.

Memority on Google Cloud Dedicated / S3NS (Audit-ready sovereign identity governance): Integrating Memority’s identity factory platform directly into the S3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment provides regulated entities with capabilities designed to support their NIS2 and DORA compliance requirements with the PREMI3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment. Sources indicate that mongoDB on Google Cloud Dedicated (Modern data velocity with domestic residency): Running MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on Google Cloud Dedicated gives developers the flexibility of the document model while adhering to strict regional isolation requirements. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Roadzen, which applies AI to insurance and mobility, has secured roughly $10m (₹94 crore) for its Indian subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, which is now valued at about $300m post-money on a stand-alone basis.
  • Recent findings suggest that the round is being raised entirely as common equity.
  • It has been revealed that as part of the deal, Roadzen is bringing its worldwide operating businesses together under Roadzen AI Limited, which was previously called Roadzen Technologies Limited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roadzen, which applies AI to insurance and mobility, has secured roughly $10m (₹94 crore) for its Indian subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, which is now valued at about $300m post-money on a stand-alone basis.

Recent findings suggest that the round is being raised entirely as common equity. It carries no warrants or preferred rights, and the fresh shares rank equally with those held by the existing shareholder, Roadzen. Because the capital goes into the subsidiary, shareholders in the Nasdaq-listed parent will not be diluted. Family offices and capital markets investors anchored the deal. Several of them had backed the firm’s earlier India subsidiary round and raised their commitments this time.

It has been revealed that as part of the deal, Roadzen is bringing its worldwide operating businesses together under Roadzen AI Limited, which was previously called Roadzen Technologies Limited. Roadzen Inc. will remain the Nasdaq-listed parent and will keep about 89% of the subsidiary.

According to recent reports, the money will go towards the group’s fastest-growing priorities in insurance and mobility. It will also shore up the balance sheet and support the organization’s aim of reaching an annual revenue run-rate of $100m this fiscal year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.
  • Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

In a recent development, IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:.

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

According to recent reports, the full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

Sources indicate that we use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:.

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it reveals that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

In a recent development, A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.

NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest raise takes the organization’s total funding to $185m.

Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was confirmed in August.

In a recent development, the funding arrives as large organisations move promptly to integrate Corma’s model into their security operations amid mounting concern over AI-driven attacks. Since the company released publicly, interest has climbed among Fortune 100, Fortune 500 and Fortune Global 500 businesses, which are handing a growing share of their security workload to Corma’s autonomous AI workforce. To keep pace, the firm has expanded its server capacity 24-fold.

At its August launch, Corma cautioned that AI was advancing far faster on the offensive side than the defensive one. That concern was borne out in October, when a series of serious vulnerabilities and breaches affecting widely used software, nicknamed “Black October,” left security teams under pressure and prompted warnings from governments in Washington, Tokyo and elsewhere.

According to Corma, the imbalance stems from the industry’s focus on coding. As leading labs pour resources into models that write software, those same models become more adept at spotting flaws, since vulnerabilities are effectively bugs. When combined with agents, they can now carry out exploits from start to finish. Defensive work outside code security, however, calls for different skills, such as sifting through large amounts of audit logs, security events and network flows, linking faint signals across systems over extended periods, and remaining consistent through long chains of decisions. Coding models were not designed for these tasks.

Corma trains foundation models specifically for this defensive work and deploys them as an AI workforce that sits alongside human security teams, operating within their existing tools and handling a broad range of security tasks.

Sources indicate that corma co-founder and CEO Alon Pluda noted, “Cybersecurity is now a battle of intelligence against intelligence, and Black October made that impossible to ignore. Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand.

Industry observers note that NEA partner Aaron Jacobson said, “Corma is building the intelligence layer that defensive security needs. As AI gives attackers an advantage, Corma’s combination of frontier AI research and deep cybersecurity expertise has the potential to help organizations defend against these threats at scale. Corma is the only company taking this on in a way that is scalable across organizations to prevent the next big cyberattack.”.

Google is a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has been recognized as a Leader and positioned furthest in vision in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems (Cloud ODBMS).
  • This recognition comes as we cross into the era of agentic AI.
  • Powering a true System of Action through the Agentic Data Cloud requires operational data to be unified, open, and inseparable from the AI tier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Google has been recognized as a Leader and positioned furthest in vision in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems (Cloud ODBMS).

This recognition comes as we cross into the era of agentic AI. Leading enterprises are in their journey of deploying autonomous agents to transform core business functions. At the center is data, the fuel for AI. In our view, this recognition from Gartner — particularly our placement furthest for Completeness of Vision — builds on the August 2026 Gartner® report, AI Vendor Race: Google Is the Company to Beat in Data Platforms for AI. Together, we believe this validates our long-standing belief that the future of operational data is unified, open, and inseparable from the AI layer. In our opinion, this is the blueprint for what we call the Agentic Data Cloud.

Powering a true System of Action through the Agentic Data Cloud requires operational data to be unified, open, and inseparable from the AI tier. We deliver on this across our operational databases by converging transaction processing and analytics in a single engine, while leveraging Google's full-stack AI advantage to integrate Google DeepMind models and vector indexing directly into the core engine over our AI Hypercomputer. Furthermore, we define openness not just through 100% PostgreSQL compatibility and open Apache Iceberg formats, but by providing borderless access to data across other clouds and environments without requiring complete data replication. This eliminates operational friction and costly data movement, providing the low-latency, planet-scale foundation needed to power trusted autonomous agents with confidence.

It has been revealed that the Agentic Data Cloud is engineered from the ground up to minimize the complexity and hidden costs of the agentic era. Let's review the core benefits enterprises realize when operating on Google Cloud operational databases, along with our latest innovations to help you thrive in the agentic era.

Our operational database portfolio, anchored by Spanner and AlloyDB, integrates AI natively within the database engine. In AlloyDB, auto vector embeddings and auto vector indexing automatically generate, maintain, and self-tune vector data using simple SQL commands, eliminating complex ETL pipelines. Furthermore, built-in support for Google DeepMind models such as TimesFM enables zero-shot time-series forecasting directly in SQL. With Spanner, organizations can combine full-text, vector, and graph capabilities in a single database to power complex multi-model agentic workflows and context-aware applications with enterprise-grade availability.

In the companion 2026 Gartner® Critical Capabilities for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems report, Google’s operational database portfolio was evaluated as Google (Spanner) and Google (AlloyDB) for the following use cases.

Industry observers note that agentic AI Operations use case: Google was ranked first among all evaluated vendors, with Google (Spanner) ranking #1 and Google (AlloyDB) ranking #2. Capabilities such as natively built AI functions provide developers the ability to bring the power of foundational models within operational databases.

It has been revealed that OLTP Transactions use case: Google (Spanner) placed #2 among all evaluated vendors. Spanner's horizontal scalability with full interoperability between various modalities and no-compromise strong consistency enables differentiated experiences.

In addition, Google (Spanner) placed among the 3 highest-scoring vendors across all 4 evaluated use cases in the report, which we believe demonstrates the breadth of workloads it supports across transactional, analytical, NoSQL, and agentic AI scenarios.

Industry observers note that your organization's ability to take advantage of AI depends directly on your enterprise data strategy. Autonomous agents require a modern data foundation that pairs high-performance transactional processing with in-database intelligence and vector capabilities. Google Cloud continues to set the benchmark for enterprise PostgreSQL, delivering high performance and seamless scalability, 100% PostgreSQL compatibility, and enterprise-grade reliability and security, built for agents with AlloyDB for PostgreSQL.

Sources indicate that A recent component of this data and AI foundation is PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB. Autonomous agents require real-time data to reason effectively, but their unpredictable and bursty query patterns can degrade performance if not isolated from operational systems. Purpose-built for this challenge, AlloyDB enables real-time data access with complete compute and I/O isolation. Powered by Google’s Colossus distributed storage, it dynamically provisions sandboxed reader instances in seconds—scaling to thousands of nodes, up to 3 million queries per second, and over 8 million IOPS—and scales back to zero when tasks finish. Paired with direct Iceberg access, agents can seamlessly operate across both live transactional data and analytical lakehouse tables in place with zero ETL.

It has been revealed that traditional databases have struggled to keep up with the velocity of AI development, burdened by slow provisioning, CI/CD bottlenecks, and high idle infrastructure costs. AlloyDB Express solves this with an ultra-fast, cost-effective PostgreSQL configuration purpose-built for AI coding agents, rapid prototyping, and ephemeral developer environments. Instances spin up in under two seconds and automatically scale to zero when idle, letting developers and agents iterate rapidly without paying for unused compute. When an application is ready for production, AlloyDB Express provides a seamless, one-click in-place upgrade to AlloyDB—unlocking enterprise-grade scale, high availability, and security while preserving all schemas, data, and connection endpoints.

Spanner's unified multi-model architecture converges relational, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities within a single, planet-scale operational foundation. Graph database structures have rapidly become essential for agentic workloads due to their ability to model complex, interconnected enterprise knowledge and relationships in real time. Spanner Graph enables people to execute 14 popular graph algorithms — spanning centrality, community detection, similarity, and path finding — directly through the ISO Graph Query Language (GQL). To prevent performance degradation on production workloads, these algorithms run on a fully managed, isolated compute environment while Data Boost serverlessly transfers graph data. This zero-ETL architecture delivers deep structural analytics and high-performance graph processing without impacting live transactional performance.

Spanner’s columnar engine enables lightweight analytics on the most recent updated data in Spanner. Large analytical queries that require joining analytical data in BigQuery with the latest operational data from Spanner are done leveraging Data Boost, which ensures no impact to  Spanner’s transactional workloads. Complementing these capabilities, the recent launch of Spanner queues brings native transactional messaging directly into Spanner, enabling teams to manage asynchronous background work and orchestrate complex, multi-agent workflows without dual-write complexity.

This unified data ecosystem bridges the gap between intelligence and execution, allowing automated insights to immediately trigger real-time actions back into your critical business applications and operational workflows.

Industry observers note that to prevent vendor lock-in and help ensure their long-term viability, enterprise AI deployments require a foundation of open standards and hybrid deployment flexibility. Google Cloud operational databases empower teams to run critical workloads across any environment.

According to recent reports, at the foundation of this borderless architecture, Google Cloud databases integrate into the lakehouse ecosystem by delivering unified, zero-ETL access to operational and analytical data. Through native support for open table formats like Apache Iceberg, operational databases such as AlloyDB and Spanner bridge real-time transaction processing with lakehouse analytics. This enables autonomous agents to query, reason over, and act upon live enterprise data instantly across hybrid and multi-cloud environments, minimizing data silos while maintaining strict governance, transactional consistency, and planet-scale performance.

With AlloyDB Omni and Spanner Omni, enterprises can extend Google's advanced operational database capabilities to on-premises environments, multi-cloud deployments, and air-gapped sovereign setups via Google Distributed Cloud (GDC). This helps ensure full operational consistency, compliance, and sovereignty without sacrificing performance or developer velocity.

Our database portfolio has also received broader industry recognition. Recently, Google was also named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Operational Databases 2026 Vendor Assessment.

According to recent reports, “Consider Google AlloyDB when standardizing on PostgreSQL with deeply integrated AI is a priority, particularly for organizations building AI-driven search, retrieval, and agentic applications on live operational data. The platform suits enterprises that want converged transactional and analytical processing in a single engine, enterprise-grade security, and the flexibility to run the same engine across managed cloud, self-managed, and multicloud environments through AlloyDB Omni. Organizations seeking an AI-native operational database backed by Google's ecosystem will find AlloyDB a practical option for balancing modernization, AI readiness, and operational simplicity.”.

Across Spanner and AlloyDB, we believe this recognition reinforces our mission to deliver a true System of Action built to power autonomous enterprise agents at scale.

To learn more about our placement and how we believe we innovate on behalf of our customers, download the complimentary 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Database Management Systems report.

The company plans to use the fresh capital to speed up work on its proprietary payroll engine and bring it to market more widely. It also intends to push beyond its current focus on logistics and delivery, moving into other sectors with high staff turnover, including hospitality, retail and cleaning services. Valeria’s ambition is to become the leading player in Spain’s workforce management market, which is estimated to be worth over €1bn.

Recent findings suggest that according to the tech giant, payroll processing in Spain remains heavily dependent on manual tasks handled by a scattered mix of providers, an approach that struggles in industries such as delivery, logistics and hospitality where headcounts shift weekly. Valeria pairs its in-house payroll calculation engine and AI with a dedicated team of employment law specialists, who track irregularities and provide clients with legal assurance.

Unlike most HR software, which depends on outside providers, Valeria’s system links through APIs directly to the Spanish Social Security system, the State Public Employment Service (SEPE) and the Spanish Tax Agency. Its engine handles every step automatically, covering recruitment, contract creation, sick leave notices, wage garnishments and workplace accident reporting. It also addresses the collective agreement rules applying to the courier, delivery and fleet management industries.

Set up in 2024 by CEO Pau Laporte, COO Carlos Saiz and CTO Sergio Morales, Valeria now serves over 100 businesses and 20,000 workers. The organization has expanded to a headcount of more than 40 across payroll, product and engineering since establishing its Barcelona base. Its customer roster includes Glovo, Uber Eats, Goiko, Honest Greens and Desigual.

Industry observers note that valeria CEO and co-founder Pau Laporte said, “Our focus is not on rigid corporate structures, but on businesses that need flexibility and the ability to respond immediately. Valeria’s system is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, allowing businesses to operate whenever they need to, without having to wait for manual processes or intermediaries.”.

Recent findings suggest that goHub Ventures partner Pablo Perea mentioned, “We met Pau, Carlos, Sergio, and the rest of the team more than a year ago, and watching them work since then is what has convinced us: they complement each other like few teams we have seen, and they iterate at incredible speed. In high-turnover sectors, labor management still relies on manual processes, and Valeria solves that problem with an AI-native solution that brings savings and agility to both employers and workers. We are delighted to support them as they become the benchmark in Spain and replicate the model in international markets.”.

GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visibility and context on the threats that matter most.
  • Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor.
  • As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks, automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking, the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Visibility and context on the threats that matter most.

Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor.

As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks, automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking, the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this enhancement, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed.

Key trends over the last quarter include:.

Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.

Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse: Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from LLMJacking by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers).

LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO): State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution.

Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution: Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution.

Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild.

At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through proactive disruption of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments.

While previous milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now observed multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions.

Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a upcoming defensive challenge.

Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks.

It has been revealed that in addition to the now highly-publicized pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.

GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.

CAIRN: an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US.

CyberStrikeAI: an open source, LLM-native offensive framework which functions as a "single pane of glass" for cyber operations. The core architecture consists of a Go-based backend API acting as a C2 and orchestration server and connects commercial and open-weight LLMs to over 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts to automate end-to-end attack chains.

HexStrike AI: an open source offensive Model Context Protocol (MCP)-integrated harness that enables LLM clients to directly connect to over 150 pre-installed offensive security tools. Operating through a dual-component architecture, the framework wraps standard utilities across reconnaissance, web application testing, exploitation, and binary analysis into callable functions coordinated by more than 12 specialized autonomous sub-agents.

According to recent reports, pentAGI: an open source autonomous offensive framework designed to lower technical barriers for entry-level operators running complex campaigns. Between late August and early October 2026, GTIG tracked a threat actor using a customized attack orchestration platform built off of the open source version of PentAGI used to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia.

We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations. These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation.

Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating upcoming exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally. Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions. Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they presently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.

Figure 2: LLM maturity timeline.

Google Security Operations (SecOps) has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework specifically designed to counter the speed and scale advantage of adversaries using LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

The integration of autonomous LLM agents into vulnerability research and software security workflows has shifted from theoretical experimentation to active operational deployment.

Recent findings suggest that adversaries are leveraging multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipelines to automate labor-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, such as differential patch examination, dynamic protocol fuzzing, and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization. By chaining these capabilities together, threat actors can dramatically reduce the window between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws. In contrast, searching for zero-day vulnerabilities requires casting a wider net. LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organizations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don't, creating additional verification work for defenders.

For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August.

Figure 3: Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026.

In our previous report, we detailed nascent efforts by threat actors surrounding LLM-augmented vulnerability research, including partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation attack sequences.

In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.

More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent, that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

Figure 4: Agentic framework inspecting access control implementations in the Spectra (Ultimate Addons for Gutenberg) WordPress plugin, version 2.19.25.

It has been revealed that open source research corroborates threat actor operationalization of fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines. For example, in late August 2026, threat actors exploited two vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers as zero-days that, when chained together, allow for unauthenticated remote code execution: CVE-2026-81578, an authentication bypass flaw; and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe dynamic class loading vulnerability. Using LLMs, security researchers and the cybersecurity tech giant Huntress generated working exploits for the vulnerabilities within a day of disclosure. Greynoise reported a campaign that took place four days after the initial disclosure in which a threat actor likely used LLMs to build and test exploits for these vulnerabilities, assemble a target list, and execute a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations. Greynoise also highlighted the speed of execution, noting that the threat actor expanded an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes.

The PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) also highlight several of these trends. They were discovered using LLM-enabled analysis. Before official patches were released on Oct. 21, 2026, a POC video and early patched code were published. This allowed both researchers and attackers to compare code versions, understand the flaws and attempt to build exploits before the patch became available. In the initial days following the official patch, hundreds of claimed but non-functional POCs, likely generated with the help of LLMs, were published. This proliferation created significant work for the security community to verify or debunk the POCs while monitoring for evidence of confirmed exploitation.

Google continuously invests in AI innovation and research, helping to ensure AI is built responsibly, and that we’re leveraging its potential to automatically find risks. In 2024 we introduced Significant Sleep, an AI agent developed by Google DeepMind and Google Project Zero, that actively searches and finds unknown security vulnerabilities in software. Google Cloud employs a defense-in-depth model that combines rigorous code reviews and secure-by-default libraries with continuous, automated scanning using specialized AI agents such as CodeMender to discover, patch, and remediate vulnerabilities before and after release. We partner with the global security community by running a Vulnerability Reward Program and maintaining Project Zero to proactively find and patch zero-day vulnerabilities.

GTIG assesses with high confidence that information operations (IO) threat actors have advanced from initial LLM experimentation to full operational integration. Across all tracked categories—state-sponsored groups, including those attributed to Russia, the PRC, and Iran, commercial "Influence-as-a-Service" (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks—adversaries now routinely embed LLMs into their standard tradecraft to produce synthetic media and automate domain network workflows (e.g., LLM-assisted SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of influence content). This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is vital to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success.

State-sponsored groups are IO actors directly linked to state apparatuses and have traditionally formed the primary baseline tracked by platform defenders and researchers. To preserve plausible deniability, they increasingly rely on third-party commercial contractors to execute campaigns on their behalf.

In a recent development, commercial IaaS vendors encompass marketing and PR agencies, private intelligence contractors, and offshoots of commercial surveillance vendors, selling services ranging from tailored influence campaigns to turnkey platforms. Tradecraft varies across this ecosystem; intelligence contractors and surveillance offshoots in particular often apply stronger operational security (OPSEC) and more advanced techniques than traditional state-sponsored actors.

Recent findings suggest that inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are driven by profit rather than ideology. These actors generate a high volume of political clickbait to drive engagement, maximize click-through rates, and boost ad revenue. This combination of political framing and high-volume synthetic content creates a significant frontend perception gap, making IPM network campaigns the most prone to being misidentified as state-sponsored operations.

Industry observers note that as automated content generation reduces a primary operational bottleneck, adversaries are increasingly shifting their focus toward leveraging LLMs for infrastructure design, automated distribution pipelines, and anti-detection mechanisms. Specifically, our observations indicate a notable shift toward the commercial development of LLM-enabled, end-to-end IaaS platforms designed to support and automate the full influence campaign lifecycle. The proliferation of these platforms can lower operational overhead for state and commercial actors while increasing the difficulty of detecting coordinated and inauthentic behavior across social media platforms.

In August 2026, GTIG investigated threat activity leveraging the Gemini API alongside tools from multiple AI providers to build an end-to-end IaaS platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, primarily across Europe and the Middle East. The platform was engineered to automate the entire IO campaign lifecycle, including persona creation, multimodal media generation, automated content distribution, and interactive posting across platforms. Identified prompts reflected an operational focus on emulating organic grassroots engagement (i.e., “astroturfing”) while evading platform detection rules.

Identified prompts instructed models to adopt localized personas specific to targeted geography, mimicking regional dialects and slang, while incorporating informal phrasing and intentional typos to avoid sounding like an automated tool.

Prompts supporting media generation introduced deliberate camera flaws simulating realistic photos typically captured by smartphone cameras (e.g., making images appear grainy or incorporating uneven lighting changes) and omitted background text to avoid synthetic image markers.

GTIG also detected a separate commercial contractor leveraging the Gemini API—as part of a modular, multi-provider AI architecture—during the development of a turnkey IaaS platform engineered to manage over 100,000 accounts across major global platforms. The platform is architected to combine automated agents, anti-detection and device identifier spoofing tools, and cloud phone farms to operate thousands of inauthentic personas across platforms. Observed prompts indicated the actor’s proposal to market the tool to both the actor’s domestic government bodies and foreign clients for influence campaign execution.

To manage large volumes of social media accounts, the platform was designed to run virtual smartphones in cloud environments—disguising each virtual device as a legitimate mobile device—and route web traffic through proxies to bypass automated bot detection and rate limits.

The architecture additionally includes automated fake account creation using disposable email addresses and overseas virtual SMS numbers. To avoid further suspicion, newly-created accounts were configured to undergo an automated aging period, leveraging LLMs to simulate realistic user behavior (e.g., how long a user lingers on a post, scrolling, and interacting with non-campaign content) to establish a history of normal activity before pushing targeted messaging.

Recent findings suggest that alongside the development of IaaS software suites, threat actors continue to integrate commercial LLM tools into baseline content workflows to overcome linguistic barriers, customize messaging, and scale output. Using commercial models to produce commentary, synthetic personas, and stylized animations at the content layer allows IO actors to improve the credibility and demographic resonance of their campaigns, while enabling IPM networks to mass-produce political clickbait for advertising revenue.

According to recent reports, LLM-Enabled Quality Enhancement in Long-Running IaaS Campaign: Since our last report, GTIG observed a long-running IaaS provider tracked since 2019 leveraging LLMs to elevate the baseline quality and volume of its influence operations. Utilizing a proprietary software suite designed to manage thousands of synthetic profiles across major platforms, the provider targeted political discourse in multiple countries. Operators integrated LLM models to produce more convincing virtual personas, as well as academic-style commentary and media focused on political, religious, and civil rights topics. The resulting content was subsequently promoted and amplified across platforms using fabricated Western personas.

Demographic Targeting via Synthetic Content: We have observed threat actors using LLM-generated content to customize context for specific regions and audiences, for example by using synthetic influencer personas to promote policy narratives targeting specific demographics. A separate network posted synthetic, Lego brick-inspired animations and football parodies to satirize global political figures, likely in an attempt to appeal to younger audiences by effectively packaging propaganda in short-video formats consistent with popular internet culture.

It has been revealed that LLM-Augmented Inauthentic Political Monetization (IPM): GTIG also tracks a growing trend of IPM actors using LLMs to mass-produce political content. Although their thematic focus, quality, and volume can resemble state-backed IO campaigns, these non-ideological operations exploit societal polarization solely to maximize engagement, click-through rates, and advertising revenue. GTIG has observed IPM operators prompting commercial LLMs to identify lucrative political topics, trending keywords, and high-Cost Per Mile (CPM) niches for ad monetization, while promoting the resulting content via synthetic news anchors that occasionally spoof the likenesses of real journalists and commentators to manufacture credibility.

Recent findings suggest that GTIG collaborates closely with product teams to take action against IO actors across affected Google surfaces under our standard platform policies. Our research and rigorous analysis enables Google teams to make enforcement decisions and to disrupt coordinated IO campaigns. GITG, YouTube, and Google Trust & Safety track and regularly enforce on accounts associated with coordinated IO posting content and commenting. Examples of this enforcement include disruption of YouTube channels, blogs, AdSense accounts, and domains removed from Google News surfaces, as we report on a quarterly basis in the Influence Operations Bulletin.

Beyond enforcement actions, GTIG shares insights with Google DeepMind to harden our platforms and services against emerging tradecraft. This intelligence is used to establish abuse baselines, enhance Gemini’s ability to recognize and refuse misuse, and inform internal policy modifications.

While compromised credentials have long served as the fundamental bedrock for initial access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement during intrusions, adversaries are increasingly repurposing stolen credentials and compute resources to power unauthorized LLM tooling and autonomous operational pipelines. As access costs, token rate limits, and geographic restrictions present persistent operational hurdles for threat actors attempting to scale LLM capabilities, adversaries are actively harvesting session tokens and platform credentials directly from victim endpoints and continuous integration environments. In tandem with this shift toward hijacking valid credentials for LLMs, underground cybercrime forums and illicit marketplaces have rapidly matured to meet this demand—transitioning beyond generic identity dumps to commodifying verified frontier AI accounts, tokenized API quotas, and targeted infostealer configurations as turnkey utilities for downstream exploitation.

Sources indicate that throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents where financially motivated actors compromised cloud environments to consume targeted organizations’ cloud compute and/or LLM resource quotas. As seen in the image below, LLMJacking can generate significant usage and billing increases within hours. In some cases, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000 USD. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation.

Figure 5: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests.

In November, Mandiant and GTIG described a set of common TTPs we observed across intrusions that affected financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region.

Description of Observed Tactics.

Threat actors frequently used credential theft and session hijacking to gain access to targeted environments, including harvesting valid credentials from public GitHub repositories, and social engineering using deceptive websites to trick users into providing active session tokens.

Internal Reconnaissance & Lateral Movement.

Sources indicate that seeking to identify credentials and systems of interest, attackers conducted reconnaissance against internal code repositories, data stores, cloud services, containers, and access logs. In at least one case, a threat actor exploited a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running in an internal container to navigate to additional systems.

Privilege Escalation & Persistence.

According to recent reports, threat actors created unauthorized IAM and service accounts or attached administrative policies to service roles. We also observed a threat actor exploit CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that allows an attacker to elevate limited-access inference keys ("Virtual Keys") into full administrative credentials. Privileged service accounts were sufficient to establish persistence without the use of malware.

According to recent reports, inside organizations’ cloud environments, attackers enabled LLM services, including subscribing compromised accounts to pay-as-you-go agreements. To circumvent rate limits, one threat actor used a “burn and rotate” strategy, creating and deleting short-lived service accounts. Other threat actors abused cloud compute resources, provisioning instances with powerful GPUs and requesting quota increases in order to run their own LLM tooling. This included agentic frameworks that a threat actor used to automate further exploitation of the compromised network, as well as open source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure deployed to facilitate the sale of access to the compromised organization’s resources.

Table 3: Common TTPs observed in LLMJacking intrusions.

In another investigation, we observed at least two separate attackers seeking to conduct LLMJacking operations. Both actors accessed a targeted environment using the same set of legitimate credentials, which were potentially sold or leaked on underground forums. The first threat actor used legitimate credentials to gain access to the environment, enumerate available LLM services, and query cost and usage information related to the account. On the same day, we observed a set of IP addresses using a common User-Agent, likely a botnet or proxy service, also accessing the environment using the same legitimate credentials. The botnet or proxy service generated millions of LLM API calls in approximately 24 hours before the credentials were revoked. Though the first threat actor returned to the environment, creating service accounts provisioned with permissions to query LLMs, the botnet’s noisy activity caused the compromised credentials to be remediated before this threat actor could execute LLM queries.

For hardening and mitigation guidance for defending against LLMJacking intrusions, please see our blog.

Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure. This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.

According to recent reports, the LLM Mixer ecosystem mirrors the broader cybercrime marketplace, where specialized threat groups handle discrete phases of the supply chain. While LLM Mixer operators maintain infrastructure and customer fulfillment, for example, operators may partner with separate threat actors who establish initial access to compromised environments, purchase compromised credentials from infostealer operators, or recruit partners to systematically register free trial accounts.

Recent findings suggest that GTIG analyzed numerous LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, and found that most services offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken models that advertise support of malicious cyber activity. Advertised pricing varies significantly across individual mixer platforms and based on the models and types of credentials offered; for example, free trial credentials were much cheaper than enterprise. We observed prices per million tokens range from $0.10 USD to $25 USD. One vendor, APIMart, applies a 5x price increase on both input and output once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Rather than pricing per million tokens, some vendors such as JetNight offer monthly subscriptions at differing prices based on the type of model offered.

Figure 6: APIMart advertised prices.

Industry observers note that since our last report, GTIG has continued to observe threat actors leveraging LLMs to augment various phases of the attack lifecycle. However, widespread adoption of LLM tooling also introduces significant operational drawbacks. The forensically noisy nature of many LLM tool processes can degrade OPSEC and compromise stealth, creating a detrimental impact on espionage campaigns. In addition, LLMs can reduce operational reliability, as adversaries must contend with model limitations, including the hallucination of non-existent details or even targets. Consequently, we anticipate that actors who specialize in stealthy operations designed to maintain long-term persistence are less likely to rely on forensically noisy tools within a targeted environment, though they may employ them selectively for speed and scale, depending on operational priorities. Conversely, we assess with high confidence that actors less concerned with operational stealth, including many cyber crime actors, will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates.

It has been revealed that state-sponsored threat actors continue to leverage LLMs in their respective operations, reinforcing baseline assessments communicated in our previous reports. For example, we continue to see CALANQUE ION, an Iranian government-backed actor previously tracked as APT42, leverage LLMs—including Gemini—to augment reconnaissance and targeted social engineering. We also see PRC-nexus threat actors leveraging LLMs for reconnaissance and research. In addition to this newly introduced baseline of threat actors leveraging LLMs, we observed the following activity:.

In Q3 2026, PRC-nexus cyber espionage actors used LLM tools and models for reconnaissance, front-end scanning, researching targets across various sectors and geographies, and weaponizing exploits.

We have also observed threat actors using LLMs to conduct post-compromise data analysis. This includes PRC contractor LEAKY CASTLE, which overlaps with public reporting about data leaked from a contractor using LLMs to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data, including deriving insights into organizational structures and adding them into finished intelligence reports to sell to customers.

Recent findings suggest that in a latest trend, we have observed PRC-nexus actors abusing LLM platforms and file-hosting backends for staging, dead drop C2s, and exfiltration. In one example, a threat actor abused a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents.

We also continue to see threat actors from the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) using LLM tools to support DPRK IT worker activity, such as generating resumes and preparing for job interviews at Western organizations. DPRK threat actors are also abusing generative tools for operational scaling and exploiting native agent execution hooks as enterprise access vectors.

We observed the use of public facing tools to generate responses during job screenings, allowing them to sound authentic while posing as Western IT workers to secure remote employment.

While we continue to see DPRK actors leveraging LLM-powered tools to generate lure content and assist with coding, over the course of 2026 we’ve observed an evolution of tactics. In multiple intrusions, a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE threat cluster combined LLM-enabled social engineering and abused organizations' AI tools as a supply chain attack vector.

In a recent development, in recent intrusions targeting cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe, the threat actor exploited LLM software architectures as a lateral execution surface. For initial access, the actor created fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms whose profile imagery contained SynthID watermarks, confirming use of LLMs to synthesize deceptive professional identities. These personas directed targets to fraudulent meeting platforms featuring "ClickFix" social engineering lures, which prompted targets to run diagnostic fix scripts, which executed likely LLM-authored staging scripts via ClickFix lures. Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when consumers started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor. To maintain stealth, suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE further masked its lateral movement by generating GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs) named after Microsoft Copilot, underscoring how threat actors are simultaneously abusing generative tools for operational scaling and exploiting native AI agent execution hooks as enterprise access vectors.

According to recent reports, in developments in the last quarter, in addition to the use of offensive frameworks in financially motivated activity, we observed cybercrime actors leverage LLMs to scale tooling for clients; for example, Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) operators using LLMs to create tools for low-sophisticated adversaries. The Jieyou phishing service, an active Chinese-language PhaaS platform first observed in March 2026, is primarily used by cybercriminals to deploy and manage highly convincing phishing campaigns, with a particular focus on e-commerce fraud. The service introduced an LLM chatbot assistant in its June 2026 backend revision. This chatbot allows threat actors to easily configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands, significantly lowering the technical barrier for deploying campaigns. The backend chatbot is model-agnostic and integrates with several frontier and open source platforms via APIs. The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier. Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly.

Recent findings suggest that these activities triggered Gemini's safety responses, and Google took additional, broader action to disrupt the threat actors' campaigns. Additionally, we've taken action against these actors by disabling the assets associated with this activity and making updates to prevent further misuse. Google DeepMind has used these insights to strengthen both classifiers and our models, enabling them to refuse to assist with these types of attacks.

In a recent development, google uses a multifaceted defense strategy to protect our users and infrastructure against LLM abuse, integrating proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, targeted containment protocols, and proactive red teaming to simulate and protect against threats. Additionally, as innovation moves forward, the industry needs security standards for building and deploying AI responsibly, which is why we introduced the Secure AI Framework (SAIF), a conceptual framework to secure AI systems.

It has been revealed that we continuously harden our models against misuse by feeding insights from active threat monitoring directly into our safety classifiers and guardrails. For instance, in response to model extraction—or “distillation”—attacks, we have deployed real-time defenses designed to degrade the performance of unauthorized "student" models and detect attempts to clone proprietary logic. When we identify bad actors, we take direct action to disrupt their operations by disabling associated projects and accounts.

In a recent development, to extend these protections to enterprise customers, we developed Google AI Threat Defense (AITD). This autonomous architecture operationalizes security by bringing together the reasoning power of Gemini and other frontier models, the risk prioritization of Wiz, the automated remediation capabilities of Gemini and CodeMender, and frontline intelligence from Mandiant. AITD employs a multi-model strategy that balances cost and coverage, using light models for continuous scanning and specialized frontier models for high-risk vulnerabilities.

According to recent reports, in addition to our proactive platform defenses, we’ve recently introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Google has built Gemini 4 Carbon with layered defenses against cyber misuse—combining safety training, input/output classifiers, activation-based introspection probes and chain-of-thought and agentic trajectory monitors—designed to block requests to develop functional, weaponized exploits or malware tooling. The robustness of these safeguards has been stress-tested by both internal red teams and specialized external partners including Gray Swan and Trajectory labs. Beyond the model itself, Google continuously monitors for intentional misuse in production, limits or disables access for offending accounts, and provides vetted defenders, security researchers, and government partners access to advanced dual-use cyber capabilities through the Fairwind Program. More information on the safety, security, and alignment testing conducted on Gemini 4 Carbon can be found in the Gemini 4 Carbon Safety & Security Report.

It has been revealed that google’s approach to AI is guided by a commitment to bold innovation and responsible development. Guided by our AI Principles, Google designs AI systems with robust security and safety guardrails, which are continuously tested to ensure resilience.

It has been revealed that our policy guidelines and prohibited use policies are foundational to ensuring safety. Our policy development process is built to anticipate emerging trends and design for security from the ground up, allowing us to enhance protections for users globally.

At Google, threat intelligence is a core component of our security posture. We actively investigate abuse of our platforms—including malicious cyber activities by government-backed threat actors—and collaborate with law enforcement when appropriate. Crucially, our learnings from every countermeasure we implement are fed back into our product development to improve the security for our AI models. These iterative improvements to our classifiers and model-level safeguards are vital to maintaining agility against evolving threats.

Our LLM development and Trust & Safety teams also work in constant concert with our threat intelligence, security, and modeling experts to effectively address misuse.

#525. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder
